newsitem.title: USA: FCC proposes long distance access charge reform.
newsitem.headline: FCC proposes long distance access charge reform.

text.p: The Federal Communications Commission proposed on Tuesday two alternate approaches to trim the $23 billion a year long distance companies pay to local phone companies in access fees.
But the commission ducked the contentious issue of whether or not such charges should be imposed on Internet service providers, asking for comment on the issue without offering any proposals.
In a notice of proposed rulemaking, the commission said it could impose a schedule of long distance access charge reductions or simply allow market forces to drive fees lower.

The access charges, which make up a substantial portion of local phone company revenues, were adopted after the 1982 break-up of AT&T Corp and the creation of the Baby Bells. But the Telecommunications Act of 1996 is likely to change the landscape by fostering competition at the local level.
Long distance companies charge that the access fees are excessive and they favor deep, government-mandated cuts.
Local phone companies concede that the fees exceed their actual costs in carrying long distance calls but would prefer a gradual, market-based reduction.

Under the FCC's market-based approach, new entrants in the local market would compete with the baby Bells to connect long distance calls. The FCC would gradually relax and ultimately remove price caps and access fee schedules while relying on competition to drive the fees down.

The alternate approach would recognize that maket forces alone may not be sufficient to drive access rates down, the commission said. The Commission would specify the nature and timing of changes in existing rate levels under the second approach.
Local phone companies also connect Internet users to Internet service providers over local phone lines, but they receive no access charges for those calls.
Recently, several Baby Bells have complained that Internet users are getting a free ride, tying up local lines with lengthy calls.

The FCC Tuesday did not take even a proposed position on whether or not Internet service providers should be required to pay access fees. In a less formal "notice of inquiry," the commission asked for comment on possible reform "relating to interstate information services and the Internet."
Internet service providers, seeking to attract customers with flat-rate monthly pricing plans, fear per-minute access charges would stifle development of the online world.
Comments are due by January 27 on the long distance charge proposals and by Feb 21 on the Internet issue.
Ultimately, the FCC could adopt portions of both approaches for lowering long distance access fees, the commission said.
